newsitem.title: ITALY: Europe calls for global partnership against hunger.
newsitem.headline: Europe calls for global partnership against hunger.

text.p: The European Union weighed in at the World Food Summit on Friday, advocating a global partnership to fight "the scourge and curse" of hunger.
European Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler said nations should stop trying to find "scapegoats" for malnutrition and work together to overcome it.

"Citizens in poor populated areas must do more to limit population growth whereas citizens in well-off areas must notably strive to limit over-consumption," Fischler told the summit at the U.N. Food and Agriculture Organisation headquarters.
He said the well-off citizens of the developed world should agree to "contribute personally and through their countries to help the undernourished at home and abroad".
Irish Prime Minister John Bruton, speaking on behalf of the European Union, also said trade must be balanced with aid.
"Development aid has a role in supporting national and local efforts to achieve food security," Bruton said, adding that fair trade was also important.
"If we are to feed all our people we must produce and distribute food efficiently," he said.

Bruton said hunger could only be eradicated by going to the root of the problem: poverty. He said good governance free of corruption, education and adequate health care were all factors as well as the upholding of democratic principles.
"Human rights and respect for democracy must not be seen as luxuries to be enjoyed only by those who can afford them," Bruton said.
Cuts in Western food aid rankle with many of the food-importing countries at the summit. They accuse the West of abandoning them to become victims of violent fluctuations in grain prices.
It also divides the biggest food aid donors, the EU and the United States, which have squabbled in the past over the size of their donations.

The EU last year bitterly criticised a U.S. decision to reduce funding for the amount of grain offered as foreign aid. Washington, however, says it always exceeds its minimum pledges and remains the world's leading food aid supplier.

"External support must complement food security efforts of the net food-importing developing countries," Fischler said. "We all know in our hearts that simply liberalising the agricultural market cannot be the only answer, because there are many people who cannot pay."
German Agriculture Minister Jochen Borchert echoed Fischler's position on trade.

"The liberalisation of trade has its limits, and the agricultural sector is no exception," Borchert said. But he added that future food security "will depend primarily on the developing countries' own efforts".
Baroness Lynda Chalker, Britain's minister for overseas development, said the world should stop having gatherings such as the food summit and take action instead.

"I for one -- and there are many others -- think that implementing action plans for the benefit of our fellow human beings must be at the top of all our agendas, not more summits," she said. "We've had enough of them."
